title: Release of the 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report
summary_raw:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
Press Statement


			
			


			
			
October 8, 2026
Human trafficking is a direct assault on the values of freedom and dignity that define America.  The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report reveals new ways criminal organizations and repressive regimes use this abhorrent practice for financial gain.  The report also calls for accountability for governments that fail to punish traffickers and protect their citizens.  The Trump Administration will use all available tools to fight traffickers and their enablers and bring them to justice.  
2026 Trafficking in Persons Report: https://www.state.gov/reports/2026-trafficking-in-persons-report.

title: Operation Economic Outcast Sanctions on Iran’s Shadow Fleet Network
summary_raw:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
Press Statement


			
			


			
			
October 8, 2026

Under Operation Economic Outcast, the United States is using every diplomatic and economic
tool available to isolate the Iranian regime, sever its economic lifelines, and protect the United
States, our partners, and freedom of navigation.
Today, the Department of State is taking action to dismantle Iran’s shadow fleet and the Iranian
regime’s ability to use the illicit oil trade to fund its malign activities. The Department of State is
sanctioning ten entities, six individuals, and five vessels involved in the trade of Iranian-origin
petroleum or petrochemical products.
Additionally, the Department of the Treasury is sanctioning 17 entities and their shadow fleet
vessels. These measures will deprive the Iranian regime of funds and prevent it from using the
shadow fleet to transport Iranian petroleum and petrochemicals and evade U.S. sanctions.
All Department of State targets are being sanctioned pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13846,
which authorizes and reimposes certain sanctions with respect to Iran. Treasury’s action was
taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum sector,
among other key sectors of the Iranian economy.  For more information on today’s action, please
see the Department of the Treasury’s press release and State’s Fact Sheet.

title: U.S. Intensifies Operation Economic Outcast Against Iran’s Shadow Fleet Network
summary_raw:
Office of the Spokesman
Fact Sheet


			
			


			
			
October 8, 2026
Today under President Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast, the Department of State is further dismantling this illicit network and cutting off the Iranian regime’s ability to fund its malign activities.  The Department of State is sanctioning ten entities, six individuals, and five vessels in connection with trade in Iranian-origin petroleum, petroleum products, and petrochemical products.
All Department of State targets are being designated pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13846, which authorizes and reimposes certain sanctions with respect to Iran.
Sanctioning Traders of Iranian-Origin Petrochemical Products 
NOORZAD PETROKIMYA URUNLERI NAKLIYE SANAYI VE TICARET LIMITED SIRKETI (NOORZAD PETROKIMYA) is a Türkiye-based petrochemical trading company that imported and purchased approximately $3.8 million in Iranian-origin petrochemical products between January and July 2024.  SAID AHMAD NOORZAD (NOORZAD) is a Turkish national and the director and Chief Executive Officer of NOORZAD PETROKIMYA. 





  NOORZAD PETROKIMYA URUNLERI NAKLIYE SANAYI VE TICARET LIMITED SIRKETI is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.  





  NOORZAD is being blocked pursuant to section 5(a)(vii) of E.O. 13846 as a principal executive officer, or person performing similar functions and with similar authorities, of NOORZAD PETROKIMYA.  




ARABIANPRO MATERIALS FZCO is a United Arab Emirates-based petrochemical trading company that exported $2 million in Iranian-origin petrochemical products between February 2025 and July 2025.





  ARABIANPRO MATERIALS FZCO is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.




SSPL SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED (SSPL SOLUTIONS) is an India-based petrochemical trading company that imported $2 million in Iranian-origin petrochemical products between February 2025 and July 2025.  DHWANI NISARG VORA is an Indian national and a director of SSPL SOLUTIONS.  NISARG SAMIR VORA is an Indian national and a director of SSPL SOLUTIONS.





  SSPL SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.





  DHWANI NISARG VORA is being blocked pursuant to section 5(a)(vii) of E.O. 13846 as a principal executive officer, or person performing similar functions and with similar authorities, of SSPL SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED.  





  NISARG SAMIR VORA is being blocked pursuant to section 5(a)(vii) of E.O. 13846 as a principal executive officer, or person performing similar functions and with similar authorities, of SSPL SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED. 




BGZ DIS TICARET LIMITED SIRKETI (BGZ) is a Türkiye-based petrochemical trading company that imported approximately $20 million in Iranian-origin petrochemical products between January and September 2024, including $2 million from Iran-based PADIDEH PLASTIC POSHTIBAN COMPANY. 





  BGZ is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.  




PADIDEH PLASTIC POSHTIBAN COMPANY (PADIDEH) is an Iran-based petrochemical trading company that exported approximately $2 million in Iranian-origin petrochemical products between April and August 2024 to Türkiye-based BGZ.





  PADIDEH is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.  




TUTER PLASTIK SANAYI VE TICARET LIMITED SIRKETI is a Türkiye-based petrochemical trading company that imported approximately $3.5 million in Iranian-origin petrochemical products between January 2023 and August 2024.





  TUTER PLASTIK SANAYI VE TICARET LIMITED SIRKETI is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.  




Continued Targeting of Iran’s Dark Fleet and Service Providers
SAMUDRA MARINE SERVICES PRIVATE LIMITED (SAMUDRA) is an India-based customer broker that facilitated the import of multiple shipments of Iranian-origin petrochemical products to India.  KETAN MANOHAR KOCHIKAR (KOCHIKAR) is an Indian national and a director of SAMUDURA.  BHUPENDRASINGH DHALSINGH SAHU (SAHU) is an Indian national and a director of SAMUDRA.  HARISHYAM HARIHARAN CHUNDAKATTIL (CHUNDAKATTIL) is an Indian national and a director of SAMUDRA. 





  SAMUDRA is being designated pursuant to Section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.  





  KOCHIKAR is being blocked pursuant to section 5(a)(vii) of E.O. 13846 as a principal executive officer, or a person performing similar functions and with similar authorities, of SAMUDRA.





  SAHU is being blocked pursuant to section 5(a)(vii) of E.O. 13846 as a principal executive officer, or a person performing similar functions and with similar authorities, of SAMUDRA.





  CHUNDAKATTIL is being blocked pursuant to section 5(a)(vii) of E.O. 13846 as a principal executive officer, or a person performing similar functions and with similar authorities, of SAMUDRA.




ONE PLUS INTERNATIONAL CO LTD is the United Kingdom-based registered owner of YONG TAI (IMO 9231511).  YONG TAI, a Gambia-flagged Oil Products tanker, loaded Iranian-origin methanol from Iran in December 2025.  YONG TAI loaded Iranian-origin petrochemical products on at least twelve other occasions since 2024. 





  ONE PLUS INTERNATIONAL CO LTD is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(iii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petrochemical products from Iran.  




YONG TAI is being identified as property in which ONE PLUS INTERNATIONAL CO LTD has an interest.




HORIZON SHIP MANAGEMENT FZE is the UAE-based commercial manager of YASHAR (IMO: 9129380), a Comoros-flagged LPG tanker that loaded Iranian-origin liquefied petroleum gas on at least three occasions between 2025 and 2026.





  HORIZON SHIP MANAGEMENT FZE is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(ii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petroleum or petroleum products from Iran.  





  YASHAR is being identified as property in which HORIZON SHIP has an interest.




HESSONITE SHIP MANAGEMENT LLC (HESSONITE) is the UAE-based commercial manager of ARGO MARIS (IMO: 9041643), a Honduras-flagged Asphalt/Bitumen tanker that loaded sanctioned Iranian-origin petroleum products on at least eight occasions between January 2026 and August 2026.  The other two tankers the company manages have also transported Iranian-origin petroleum products at least eight times during HESSONITE’s tenure as their commercial manager.





  HESSONITE is being designated pursuant to section 3(a)(ii) of E.O. 13846 for knowingly engaging in a significant transaction for the purchase, acquisition, sale, transport, or marketing of petroleum or petroleum products from Iran. 




ARGO MARIS is being identified as property in which HESSONITE has an interest.




BLACK MAYA (IMO: 9118800) is being identified as property in which HESSONITE has an interest.




ATHE NOVA (IMO: 9188116) is being identified as property in which HESSONITE has an interest.




SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS 
As a result of today’s sanctions-related actions, and in accordance with E.O. 13846, all property and interests in property of the sanctioned persons described above that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).  In addition, any  entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  
All transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons are prohibited unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC or exempt.  These prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any blocked person and the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  
The power and integrity of U.S. government sanctions derive not only from the U.S. government’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior. 
Petitions for removal from the SDN List may be sent to: OFAC.Reconsideration@treasury.gov. Petitioners may also refer to the Department of State’s Delisting Guidance page.

title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel at a Joint Press Availability
summary_raw:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
Paulo Rangel, Portuguese Foreign Minister
Lisbon, Portugal
Palacio das Necessidades
Remarks


			
			


			
			
October 8, 2026








MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Good afternoon.  We’re going to start the press conference.  I will give the floor now to His Excellency Minister of State and Foreign Affairs Paulo Rangel.  
FOREIGN MINISTER RANGEL:  Welcome to Lisbon, Secretary Marco Rubio.   
(Via interpreter) Portugal and the United States are historic allies which together have enjoyed a lengthy relationship which defends state of law, democratic values which represent the free world, and we have strong links in economy, defense, economy, and culture.   
Obviously, I want to once again highlight the 250 years of American independence, remembering that the independence was done with Portuguese wine from Madeira, and we were the third country in the world which recognized the independence of the United States of America.  This historic friendship of allies consolidated in ‘95 with the cooperation agreement and defense agreement, which brings together the bilateral commission, which is functioning on a permanent basis.  And this bilateral commission has been a diplomatic channel of privilege for dialogue with a legal basis on many areas of our relationships, and with the military presence of the United States in the Lajes air base.   
This visit takes place at a time of great, big developments in our bilateral relations, especially in key areas like the economy and tourism.  The interest of the United States and of United States citizens and their companies to Portugal continues to grow.  In ‘25, United States visitors brought in 11 percent of revenue from tourism, and in the first quarter of ‘26, U.S. citizens were ranked third as visitors to Portugal.   
In the economy, our companies increasingly present in the United States, whether in renewable energies, pharmaceuticals, car industry.  And we have also increased investment of – United States investment in Portugal like Goldman Sachs, Aquaterra, UPS, IBM, AWS, Google have a very strong presence in our country and obviously the United States, for us, our strategic partner.  And as a member of the EU, Portugal is surely one of the countries which is a champion of the priorities that Europe should give to the transatlantic relationship.   
As part of that transatlantic relationship, Portugal agrees and agreed with your appeal from the United States for Europeans, members of NATO, to guarantee their responsibilities for their defense.  And so we have been made a effort in our budget, which has reached 2 percent of GDP in ‘25, and so a transition of 1.6 to 2 percent in a very difficult year.  And we will continue to comply with objectives of NATO, which are the 5 percent objective in medium-term future, with 3.5 in defense and 1.5 in investments related to defense sector.  For us, NATO is a fundamental pillar of our defense and our safety, our security, and so is one of our priorities in foreign policy.   
Obviously, we continue to believe that our relationship with the United States is fundamental.  We have always supported Ukraine, and we believe that the contribution of the United States is decisive in that conflict to reach a long-lasting and fair peace.  In the Middle East, we recognize the threats and the risks created by Iran and their proxies.  We defend full respect for the integrity of our friends, states in the Gulf, and we have to – essential to recover free maritime movements in Hormuz and total respect for the rule of the sea.  And the contribution of the United States is essential to solve this conflict.   
When we prepared our mandate for the Security Council, we established relations and contacts with all members of the Security Council and other states of the United Nations, and obviously we have been discussing and preparing our presence with the United States, where obviously the majority of our positions converge.   
Today, which is so important for our bilateral relationship, I’d like to welcome you especially – the important Portuguese community that lives in the United States; and they’ve been from one coast to the other – and welcome the new, enormous, and dynamic, visible U.S. citizen community in Portugal that have contributed to a new stage, a new dynamic thrust to our 50-year relationship – 243, in fact.  Thank you, Marco Rubio. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you.  I almost understood everything he said.  I almost – like, I got very close because it’s very similar to Spanish.  And so I almost turned this thing off but I said no, let me just finish it.  So anyway, but thank you.  I appreciate you having me here in your beautiful country, and I’m glad to be here.  It’s my first visit ever and I hope it will not be my last.  And I appreciate the welcome you’ve given us – not just in this extraordinary setting but the opportunity to meet with you and obviously, of course, to meet previously with – before this meeting with the prime minister.   
Our two countries have accomplished many things together in the past, and we look forward to deepening and building that relationship in the future.  In the past, for example, we’ve worked very closely on forging the arsenals of our allied forces.  We together built your F-16 fleet, strengthening not just our two nations’ security and defense, but frankly strengthening NATO as a result of it.  This is through decades of shared maintenance and training and joint operations, and we know that that will continue.   
We applaud you, by the way, on the work – and I know it’s difficult, but the commitment that you’ve made that you’re living up to in spending more – and I don’t even want to use the term spending more – in investing more on defense, and for being on track to meet all of the commitments that were made at The Hague in – by the year 2035.  And I always highlight this, because people sometimes view this call to invest more in defense as a hostile thing.  It is not a hostile thing.  On the contrary, what we are arguing is that NATO is important.  For NATO to matter, NATO has to be strong.  For NATO to be strong, NATO’s member-states need to be strong.  And for members – for NATO’s member-states to be strong, they have to have capabilities.   
Now, every country is of a different size and proportion.  Some countries can contribute more than others.  But every country in NATO needs to be as strong as they can possibly be.   Because the stronger the members of NATO are, the stronger NATO is, the stronger the Alliance is, and the stronger the deterrence is.  NATO exists, more than anything else, as a defensive Alliance that acts as a deterrent against hostility, and it has served us well for decades.  And if we want it to continue to serve us, we need to make sure that it is strong.   
So we look forward to the burden – to the – we look to share the burden of defense in the future, and we look forward to collaborating on constructing the next generation of weaponry that’s going to be needed and advanced military technology that’s going to be needed in order to deter the adversaries of the future.  I believe working together, along with all of our Allies and partners in NATO, we can make our nations and our continents safer from foreign threats and more secure for our people. 
Now, I don’t want to focus this relationship solely on our defense cooperation, because what happens between our countries goes far beyond that.  And I want to talk a little bit about the economic realm, where Portugal plays an integral role in fostering U.S. commerce and in delivering U.S. technology to the European continent and beyond.  As an example, Portugal’s undersea cables, affordable energy, critical mineral reserves, and hyperscale data centers make it the ideal gateway – the ideal gateway from a geographic and economic perspective – the ideal gateway for American technology companies to enter Europe. 
I think it’s also important to point to the amount of investment that’s going on in our respective countries.  Last year, investors from the United States invested over $20 billion in Portugal.  And Portuguese companies invested over $2 billion in the United States, which is a big number for a country of this size.  So if you think about that, that’s only going to grow and we have ideas on how that’s going to continue to grow.   
And so our governments are going to continue to make the necessary pathways for future investment in the critical industries – things like super intelligence and aerospace and defense and other strategic sectors.  And one way we intend to do that, hopefully very soon, is through a CEO forum that I know our ambassador – who is doing a great job – has been working on.  It’s a forum that gives businesses in our two respective countries a mechanism to cut through the red tape, cut through any sort of bureaucratic impediments that exist, and turn the existing connections into more investment, into more jobs, into more economic growth on both sides of the Atlantic. 
Together, we have many opportunities to expand the commercial diplomacy and relations between our two countries in ways that will bring not only profit and prosperity to our people, but I think also bring resilience and the security that comes with resilience against future economic and technological risks.   
I also want to point, for a moment, to the number of U.S. travelers that come here.  The number is stunning.  And what I learned even earlier is that, despite how many direct flights we have from the United States here, if they added more flights they could fill more seats.  So a lot of Americans want to come and visit here and not just to do business, but to visit and to see the beauty of your country and all that it has to offer and the richness of its history and so forth, and I hope that that will continue.  We also have a growing number of American retirees that are coming here as well, and I hope – that’s an important component, and I know our embassy does an excellent and hard – it’s a hard but excellent job of – in consular services and responding to all of that.   
Finally, let me say this.  I want to complement Portugal – something we don’t talk enough about, and that is on your growing and successful efforts to combat narcoterrorism, not just in your country but around the world.  In the last two years, Portugal has seized nearly 200 tons of cocaine, including approximately – what is that?  A robot?  Was that – did you see that?  Okay.  Sorry.  I’m easily distracted, guys.  We’re talking about cocaine, so let’s go back to that.  (Laughter.)  
For nearly two years – so 200 – Portugal has seized 200 tons of cocaine, including approximately 47 tons to date in 2026.  And they’ve done that in partnership with the Drug Enforcement Agency of the United States.  And in addition, Portugal’s been partnering with multiple countries in the Western Hemisphere to combat drug trafficking and transnational criminal drug organizations.  So we applaud you and we thank you for your serious response to these threats to national security.  
We’ve been partners for a very long time, as you pointed out.  Our consulate in Ponta Delgada has been there since 1795.  And that makes it the oldest continuously operating American consulate in the world – in the world.  So I look forward to future centuries of American-Portuguese collaboration as we create a more secure, stronger transatlantic alliance and foster a more prosperous future for our people.  Thank you.   
MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Now, as agreed, we will have questions from the press, United States press first, Eric Martin from Bloomberg and then Alex Raufoglu from Radio Free Europe. 
QUESTION:  Thank you.  Thank you, Secretary.  Obrigado, Ministro. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, I hate this guy.  This guy always speaks the language of the country we’re going to.  Do you know Portuguese?  (Laughter.)  
QUESTION:  Um pouquinho. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay.  
QUESTION:  Secretary Rubio, in the economic realm that you just mentioned, the U.S. has encouraged countries in the EU to work to reduce dependencies on China.  I’m wondering if that’s something you discussed with Minister Rangel or Prime Minister Montenegro here in Lisbon, or in the meetings with Greek officials this week.  And do you and your European counterparts see the challenge differently?   
(Via interpreter) One question for Minister Rangel.  You have invested in key sectors, including renewable energy.  The question of investment in these strategic infrastructure in Portuguese state companies, as Secretary of State has mentioned – are you going to impose new restrictions on these strategic sectors?   
Thank you. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  What a show-off.  This is good?  Is it a good – is he good in Portuguese?  
FOREIGN MINISTER RANGEL:  Yes.    
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay, good.  I understood.  He’s asking basically same question.  So let me start first, and that is – look, here’s our thing.  Because you focused on China, let me just say it this way.  We think it’s not good for us, for Portugal, for any country in the world to present – to depend on any country for 95 percent of anything, your pharmaceuticals, your – we think there needs to be diversity.   
And we learned that the hard way during COVID.  You saw during the pandemic, there were things that we took for granted that weren’t available to us – not because of tariffs, not because of an embargo, not because somebody – they got cut off because the supply chains were disrupted.  And we learned how dangerous it is to be over-reliant on any single part of the world for everything we get.  It is why we have spent so much time diversifying our energy portfolio.   
And even now recent events remind us that we can’t continue to rely on X percent – large percentage of the globe’s – of the world’s energy coming from a part of the world that’s often finds itself in conflict.  So I think there’s a desire on our part, as I think there is on the part of many countries, to diversify where we source things – whether it’s critical minerals or key technologies and things of that nature. 
Added to that, there is always the concern that there are certain industries that are so critical to our national security that we have to be careful about who we allow or what kind of companies we allow to invest in our economies.  This is particularly sensitive in biotechnology, but it’s also sensitive in telecommunications.  Because if your telecommunications are vulnerable to foreign companies that respond to a foreign government’s demands, then you’re – everything you do is vulnerable, because all your ability to communicate. 
And by the way, the threats to these things aren’t simply from a trade realm; they’re also kinetic.  The undersea cable security – it’s something people don’t think a lot about because you don’t see them.  Now, the undersea cables are increasingly being threatened all over the world by bad actors that are trying to access them and cut them in a time of conflict, or even as a point of leverage.   
So this comes up in every meeting we do around the world, simply because I think it’s a shared value and a shared concern that we have with many, if not all of our allies. 
FOREIGN MINISTER RANGEL:  Well, I’ll answer you in Portuguese, once you have sympathy to put the question in Portuguese.   
(Via interpreter) Just to underline what Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated, and for Portugal, the security of underwater cables is essential.  There is no meeting in which I’m present where this topic isn’t on the table.  It’s one of our major concerns exactly because we are a gateway of many undersea cables which link both sides of the Atlantic.   
Also, in answer to your question, as you know, the Portuguese relationship with China goes back 500 years.  But investment – investment in Portugal – follows our own screening, and all countries.  And that is laid down by the EU.  And to answer your question, what happens is that the EU has just approved in July and enforced new rules for screening, for screening investments.  And these rules are very sophisticated and demanding more than in the past.  And at the moment, several different ministries are working based on this new legislation, which we’ll implement this EU regulation, and which will obviously strengthen our ability to control from the point of view of security, our national interests, and vital interests, whether economic or of another nature.  And so that will be implemented as soon as this legislation is ready.  And that applies to all countries.  So it’s not just geared or directed to one.   
So we follow EU legislation and policy in this matter.  And they are discussing on a commercial basis their relations with China; there’s a Franco-German proposal.  And in that environment, we will follow the EU standards and rules.  But as regards investment, we will wait for this new legislation, which will apply to all countries.  It doesn’t affect one country or the other; it’s a European legislation, and they’re very similar to what the United States has adopted in this field. 
QUESTION:  Thank you so much.  Alex Raufoglu, Radio Free Europe.  Mr. Secretary — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, you have to answer – you have to ask your question in Portuguese.  I’m sorry.  (Laughter.) 
QUESTION:  My best in English. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right.  It was worth a try.  
QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, yesterday you urged Europe to wake from its long slumber and defend its borders.  With Russia today killing at least 33 in Ukraine, threatening Europe beyond its borders, Belarus pressuring Latvia, and a U.S. troops drawdown looming, can NATO’s eastern flank still count on — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  U.S. troops what?  U.S. troops what?  I didn’t hear. 
QUESTION:  Drawdown looming.  Can the Allies rely on American support moving — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.  Well, first of all – yeah – my speech yesterday wasn’t simply about protecting the borders.  That’s certainly critical.  When I said we want Europe to reawake from its slumber, we want Europe to recognize and remember who we are.  We are the West.  We have a lot to be proud of in our history and what our civilization has provided to the world.  And it’s something not only should we be proud of, we should be defend – we should defend.  I don’t just mean militarily defend it; I mean culturally defend it.  I mean remember who we are as a nation, remember who we are nations, remember who we are as a civilization.  That was the point of the speech. 
Now, your question about what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine – yes, this is a very dangerous war.  It’s an extremely dangerous war because, frankly, right now it seems to be at a stalemate.  And stalemates are very dangerous.  Because stalemates only end one of two ways: number one, you have a negotiated settlement, one in which each sides have to give up something in order to get peace.  And we have tried, and we will continue to try, and do what we can to facilitate a negotiated settlement to the end of that war. 
The other way that stalemates end is through escalation.  One side or the other, or both, escalate what they are doing in order to try to break the other side and break the stalemate.  And that’s very dangerous.  That’s very dangerous in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war, because that – that escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighboring countries that are members of NATO.  It could be the strikes that you’re pointing to.  It could be a number of other things that could happen that could quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict. 
So I think and I hope that the risk of escalation is one of the things that will bring both sides to the table and willing to negotiate a settlement to this war.  In the end, we do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict, to this war.  We think this war needs to end in a negotiated settlement, the sooner the better.  The United States stands ready to facilitate that.  We have tried, we will continue to try, but we’re also not going to invest in pointless processes if we can’t make progress.  In many cases, it’s proven to be counterproductive.  But we’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war that is permanent, enduring, and fair.  And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do. 
QUESTION:  If I may, the same question goes to the foreign minister as well.  If you would like to weigh in of today’s Russia’s deadly attack on Ukraine, I will be grateful.  Thanks so much.  
FOREIGN MINISTER RANGEL:  Well, I think that in my first address, I really answered to your question.  So Portugal sees the aggression of Russia as a big danger for the world, for the multilateral system, for the charter of the United Nations, for the international law.  We stand by Ukraine in a very, very clear manner.  The support in our public opinion is very, very high, probably one of the highest, in spite we are the most distant country from Ukraine in Europe.   
Then let me say that we fully agree that there’s a need to a diplomatic solution, and we support all the efforts that the United States that in this moment are, I think, the only interlocutor that is capable to find sustainable and fair peace deal.  And so of course we support these efforts and we really would like to have a solution because everybody agrees that the situation is very difficult.  We are in a stalemate in terms of the war on the ground, and the attacks, especially to Ukrainian civilians, are becoming more and more aggressive.  And so of course this shows that there’s a need to have a ceasefire, and in the meanwhile, appropriate peace agreement where these two countries can live respecting the sovereignty of each one.  And that is our message.  
MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Now the Portuguese part from Reuters and CNN, two Sergios.  First question.  
QUESTION:  (Via interpreter) Minister, question.  The new agreement to replace the old F-16s.  So the question is – has the Portuguese Government decided with political criteria or based on political criteria and not just military (inaudible), because some people say about the Portuguese air force prefers the F-35s.  And the fact that we have competition from European fighters, does that put the F-35s at a disadvantage in this tender?   
(In English) And another question for you, Mr. Secretary.  It’s the same question, obviously.  Are you confident Portugal will ultimately choose the F-35 to replace its aging F-16 fleet?  What advantages can the F-35 offer to the Portuguese air force?  And again, are you confident that the F-35 will be chosen?  
FOREIGN MINISTER RANGEL:  (Via interpreter) Easy answer.  The decision hasn’t been taken, and it’s not the foreign minister that will take that decision.  It’s all the government, including the minister of defense, that will have to answer your question.  But I can tell you obviously Portugal will decide based on our national interest.  So the criteria will be the national interest.  That will always be the underlying criteria.  
Having said that, let me add that obviously we are looking at the United States’ proposal regarding the F-35.  We are looking at it in a serious fashion like we look at others.  So I can’t add anything else because that’s not my responsibility alone.  And as you know, the minister of defense will have a large part in this decision; obviously this will be a whole government collective decision.  And because of that I can’t add anything further.  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I would just add the following.  Number one is the plane that they decide to buy for their air force to replace the F-16 is going to be up to this government, the elected representatives of the people of this country through the process they select.  They’re going to make the decision about what’s best for them.  
Now, you’re asking me as the Secretary of State of the United States which plane I think they should buy.  We think they should buy the F-35 because we think it’s the best fighter jet in the world.  And we – all we ask is a fair chance, and I think we’ll get one, to make a presentation and a proposal that will be very competitive with every other plane that is offered on the table.  In the end, they will make that decision.  Obviously, I’m not here to promote the airplanes made by some other country, so we want them to buy the F-35 and we think it’s the best plane in the world, and we’ve made these sales.   
But this sort of decision is made all over the planet.  I mean, many other countries have bought them from us as well.  So we recognize they will decide the process by which they make the selection; we just want an opportunity, and I believe we will receive the opportunity to make a very competitive presentation on why we think the F-35 is the best one.  But ultimately, they will get to choose, and we’re going to have a good relationship.   
Now, I will say there’s advantages to interoperability, having the F-35, because it’s the same system we use and we understand it.  But the choice will be theirs to make.  We think the F-35 is the best plane in the world.  We want them to buy it.  We’ll make a very good presentation.  But they’ll make the choice.  
QUESTION:  Good afternoon, Mr. Secretary.  Boa tarde, Senhor Ministro.  My first question is for the Secretary of State and it’s regarding the Lajes airfield during Epic Fury.  The public attorney has opened an inquiry regarding the use of the air base, and with concerns of violating international laws.  And Amnesty International said that Portugal should not support war crimes and the way to war crimes.  My question is:  You said that Portugal – and you gave an example – didn’t even ask for what was the mission that was passing through Lajes.  They immediately gave the authorization for that – those flights that were made by KC-35s refuelings, also F-18 Growlers, also some drones.  My question is:  Did you inform the Portuguese Government about the nature of that mission?  Because those planes flew to Lajes before and after the start of Epic Fury.   
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah —  
QUESTION:  I would like to —  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I got it.  So I can’t comment on your public – who was it again?  Your public —  
QUESTION:  Attorney.  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  — the prosecutor, yeah.  Yeah, I can’t comment on that.  That’s your internal process, so that’s not up to us to comment on.   
I – Amnesty International is a fraud.  If you’re asking me what I think what Amnesty International thinks, you know what I think Amnesty International should be focused on?  An Iranian regime that murdered, in cold blood, tens of thousands of people in the streets of Tehran and in other parts of the country.  What Amnesty International should focus on is how the Iranian regime goes into hospitals – when protesters are injured – and murders the people in their hospital bed, and by the way sometimes murders the doctors or the nurses who treated them.  So they should focus on them.  Those are war crimes.  Those are crimes against humanity, and those are crimes they’re committing against their own people.   
As far as your other questions, we have a strong, regulated relationship with Portugal, as we do with every one of our NATO Allies, and we follow those protocols every single time.  We follow those protocols.  We would never violate the sovereignty of any country.  We don’t violate the – that’s not how allies behave.  So I’m not going to get into the details of conversations that happened or didn’t happen.  Suffice it to say that we have existing protocols that govern our presence here and how we use our bases, and we always follow them out of respect and out of compliance with the agreements that we have with our NATO Allies.   
One of the advantages of the NATO Alliance – okay – I’ve been a longtime supporter of NATO, going back to my time in the Senate, because one of the arguments I always made was that NATO allowed us to have a presence in this part of the world, in Europe, that allowed us to project power in a time of crisis or contingency into other parts of the world.  That is one of the reasons why NATO is valuable to the United States.   
Not every country has sort of behaved in that way in the past.  They’ve not understood that in terms of their treatment of us.  Portugal’s been a great ally.  And we’ve had others that have been great allies, but Portugal has been a great ally.  But it’s always been a great ally within the construct of the rules and the agreements that we have in place that regulate our presence here and the use of our bases. 
QUESTION:  (Via interpreter) (Inaudible) the base in the Azores, the Lajes Air Base, and strengthening your presence in the future and the strategic position it occupies.  What’s the (inaudible)?    
FOREIGN MINISTER RANGEL:  (Via interpreter) We didn’t discuss the future of the Lajes Air Base today.  Our agenda was directed to economic issues, trade, tourism, and also dealt with a review of the major international topics.  So the bilateral relations in defense, we didn’t discuss it today because we have a bilateral commission that does that, which meets on a regular basis, as I told you at the beginning.   
And so it wasn’t discussed today because the agreement in force, the treaty in force between the two countries, has served both parties equally and fairly, so there’s no justification to talk about that.  But anything regarding the future will also be dealt with by the permanent bilateral commission, and then it will go on to a political level.  We have the right place to discuss those issues, so we didn’t need to do that today.  Thank you.   
MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Thank you for your presence.  The press conference has come to an end.

October 8, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in Lisbon today with Portuguese Prime Minister Luís Montenegro and Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel.  The Secretary underscored the enduring strength of the U.S.-Portugal alliance, rooted in more than two centuries of friendship and decades of shared service in NATO. 
The Secretary thanked Portugal for its steadfast support to U.S. forces and discussed opportunities to deepen defense-industrial cooperation.

title: United States and Zambia Sign Five-Year Global Health Partnership under the Trump Administration’s America First Global Health Strategy
summary_raw:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
Press Statement


			
			


			
			
October 8, 2026

The United States and the Republic of Zambia today signed a five-year bilateral Health Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) under the Trump Administration’s America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), a new model of health partnership built around greater Zambian investment, stronger accountability, and a clear path toward self-reliance. 
Building on more than 50 years of U.S. health assistance to Zambia, this MOU represents a $2.49 billion partnership of $1.52 billion in planned U.S. health assistance and a commitment from Zambia to invest $975 million in new funding in its own health system over five years. Under this MOU, the United States also plans to provide more than $13 million in Global Health Security funding to strengthen Zambia’s ability to detect and respond to infectious disease threats. Over five years, Zambia will progressively assume greater responsibility for its health system, including the procurement of health commodities, transitioning U.S.-supported frontline health workers into its civil service, and strengthening systems to track medicines and supplies from production to delivery. 
The United States will support Zambia in modernizing its health infrastructure, to include expanding electronic medical records and interoperable data systems for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and disease outbreak surveillance. 
The America First Global Health Strategy Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) signed to date represent more than $27.2 billion in new health funding, including more than $16.1 billion in U.S. assistance alongside more than $11.1 billion in co-investment from recipient countries, building on decades of progress fighting HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, and other infectious diseases around the world. As of October 8, the State Department has signed 36 bilateral global health MOUs with Angola, Bolivia, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cambodia, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Guatemala, Guinea, Honduras, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Panama, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra Leone, South Sudan, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Uganda, Vietnam, and Zambia.

title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
summary_raw:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
Athens, Greece
Athens International Airport
Remarks


			
			


			
			
October 8, 2026

QUESTION:  Are you asking your allies to follow America First policy or to find their own path?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I’m asking our allies to be strong.  The stronger they are, the stronger we are collectively.  That’s always been the theme.  We want a strong Europe.  We want strong partners in Europe.  We have – every country is different.  Obviously, they’re making different decisions.  But for example, in Greece, in Portugal where we’re going today, there are many countries that have stepped up – frankly, the Germans – who are stepping up and doing their part to be stronger.
The stronger – it’s a very simple concept.  It’s not very complicated, guys.  NATO is a collection of countries that have created an alliance.  The stronger the individual members of NATO are – both societally, economically, and militarily – the stronger NATO is.  And that’s what we want, and that’s what we’ve been asking for.  And I think there’s good signs in a lot of different places where that’s happening.  And obviously, there are some countries that are dragging, and I know they have a lot of domestic pressure, but I think this is good for all of us.
QUESTION:  On the reporting about your ambassador —
QUESTION:  Is there anything you wanted to – the reporting from The Wall Street Journal that Ambassador Guilfoyle had sought financial —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, guys, let me tell you something, okay?  You guys are going to ask me this.  You’re going to ask me again in Portugal.  I know the game, okay?  The game is someone gives information to a newspaper or a media outlet; the media outlet reports it.  You immediately turn to me and say, I need you to respond to our reporting.  That’s not the way this process works.  Like, our job is not to respond every time someone decides to give the media something without any advance warning, without having any chance to look at it and see what’s in there.  That’s not the way – that’s not the way you run an organization, and that’s not a serious way to conduct the policy of our country. 
So I’m not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago.  I get the game, okay?  I’ve been in this for a long time.  Within hours, some member of Congress will write you a letter demanding you answer questions to something we’ve never seen before.  I don’t even know if it’s true or not true.  So it’s just not going to work that way, and it most certainly is not going to work that way when I’m sitting in another country.  All right? 
QUESTION:  The speech last night, Mr. Secretary —
QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, doesn’t that demand an – at the very least an IG investigation?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I am – guys, I’m not playing this game with you, okay?  You guys write a story and then your editors tell you, make sure you get a comment from him on something we haven’t seen, okay?  You guys are not going to be our only source of information in the world.  I’m sorry to tell you that.  And so I want you to understand —
QUESTION:  (Inaudible.)
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, that’s not the way the process is going to work. 
QUESTION:  How does the process work then?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, first of all, the process doesn’t work like this.  We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you.  So get that out of your head, because that’s never the way it’s going to work with me.  It’s a game that’s been played for a long time, but it’s not a game we’re going to play.  We’re conducting serious business here and we’ll handle things appropriately.  I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.  You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel.  It’s not the gospel.  It’s not the gospel for me.  That’s not the way we do it. 
QUESTION:  What are your feelings as you leave Greece, sir?
QUESTION:  On your speech, why did you – why did you feel like it was important right now to deliver the message you did last night?  Can you talk about the timing of the speech?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it’s a consistent message.  I mean, the setting obviously is very unique because this is where democracy began.  This was where so many of the pillars and the foundations of the West are from.  And so it was a very unique setting obviously, and an opportunity to do it.  But I think in many ways it also, I think, reinforces our ties to Greece, which is really a model ally, and we wanted to make sure that came across as well. 
QUESTION:  Are Iranian threats constraining where the U.S. can operate in Europe and within NATO territory? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  The United States has the ability to operate – there’s nothing we – there is nothing we want or need to do against Iran that we can’t still do. 
QUESTION:  Can you compare and contrast Portugal and its support for the Iran operation with that of its immediate neighbor, Spain?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Can I compare and contrast it? 
QUESTION:  Or —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s not the purpose.  The purpose of our visit is not to start a problem with another country.  Portugal is a great ally, a very cooperative ally of the United States, a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship.  And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties.  That’s the purpose of the trip. 
QUESTION:  Okay, thank you.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right, let’s go home.  Well, not yet.  We’ve got to stop in Portugal.
QUESTION:  All right.  Thank you.
